I've read the vault's offers and pricing pages; here's the answer.

**Short answer:** Don't touch the price. Change what the customer gets. Hormozi says value goes up when you make the result bigger and more certain and make it come faster and with less effort. His sharpest lever is speed. He also argues that cutting price can lower the value people see, and that raising it often raises it.

**What he's said**

- **Value is a fraction, and price isn't in it.** On top are the dream outcome and how likely the buyer thinks they are to get it. On the bottom are how long it takes and how much effort and sacrifice it costs them. Scarcity and urgency strengthen all four. The ideal: "the moment someone says I want that thing that beautiful dream outcome they'd be virtually guaranteed they would get it it would happen immediately and it would be effortless" ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4928s) @ 1:22:08)
- **If people don't buy, fix the offer, not the price.** "if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better", and he calls it "the highest leverage thing I think you can do in the business" ([same video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5123s) @ 1:25:23)
- **Speed comes first.** "latency beats magnitude 7 days a week and twice on Sunday." Wealthy buyers care even more about time saved than money saved ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=953s) @ 15:53). His simplest move: "take whatever the delivery time you currently have is and cut it in half." He also promises premium buyers "You will always have priority. You will always be first in line." (@ 16:25)
- **Make success feel more certain.** Doing the work one-on-one in a way that doesn't scale makes buyers much more confident they'll get the result. Your reputation "acts as almost an implied guarantee", provided buyers see you as competent and well-intentioned (@ 14:12–14:45)
- **Remove effort one step at a time.** "You go through the customer experience and you take a note every time you have to do something," then delete those steps "friction point by friction point" (@ 17:00)
- **Build a 10x version.** Ask "what if we charged 10x or 100x more than your current thing? What would you include? Just go crazy with it." He notes that "many of the things that you have these ideas for don't actually cost that much" (@ 10:19). Design it as if word of mouth from this one customer were your only way to grow. Remember that "the person that's going to spend the $1,000 is a different person" (@ 13:04)
- **A higher price can add value.** "by raising the price, we actually increase the value", because buyers believe you can deliver ([video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=420s) @ 7:00). A higher price also means buyers are more invested, get better results and are less demanding. If you close more than 80% of sales, he reads that as "room in sale", meaning you're priced too low (@ 8:06)

**What he's done**
- He turned Gym Launch from a business making a few million a year at almost no profit into one making millions in profit. He did it by changing what the offer included, not by learning new skills (2023 video).
- In a 2026 consult, an HVAC duct-cleaning owner his team had advised raised prices 23% and closed more sales. Hormozi then proposed another 10%, as long as the close rate stays above the break-even point (65% in his example).

**Where this is uncertain**
- His examples come mostly from services: gyms, HVAC, coaching. The vault has little on how this applies to cheap products or commodities.
- The idea that a higher price raises trust is about trust in delivery, not luxury appeal. He frames the 10% raise as "more asking than telling", so test it rather than assume it.
- The value equation is the subject of his book *Offers*, which he sells. These videos also promote Acquisition.com.

Found the vault's leaf on this ("damaging admissions") plus the raw transcripts behind it. Here's the answer.

**Short answer:** Yes. Hormozi counts this among the strongest tools in ad copy. List every flaw prospects already complain about and state it first. Word each one as "true flaw, **but** the claim you want believed". Whatever comes after "but" is what people remember and believe.

**What he's said**

- **Why to do it.** "nothing more powerful than damaging admissions" and "of course your product isn't perfect say so" ([May 2025 copywriting talk @ 12:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=750s)). His reasoning: "what you'll sacrifice in promise you'll gain in trust and trust trumps promise" ([@ 13:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=789s)). Prospects already have these doubts: "the prospect is already thinking them". Saying them yourself earns trust, so your claims get believed afterwards ([@ 15:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=939s)).
- **The wording rule: flaw first, then "but", then the claim.** His example: "these markers smell like [ __ ] but they write four times longer than other markers and they don't dry out" ([@ 13:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=824s)). Never put it the other way round: "if I said our systems work but they're incredibly boring I'm going to emphasize on the boring part" ([@ 15:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=903s)). Other examples he gives: "our websites are ugly as hell but they convert", and "our systems are incredibly boring but they work."
- **Stack several flaws, and use humor if you can.** His gym example: "our gym has honestly pretty terrible parking our AC is kind of on and off i don't have the best equipment but our sessions are more fun than everyone else's" ([@ 15:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=939s)). He says "if you can do with humor you get even more bonus points." A plain "we have the most fun sessions" isn't believable, because "anyone can say that", but "what people won't say is the truth" ([@ 16:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=975s)).
- **Your homework, in his words:** "write down all of the flaws all the things that people complain about the things that you know you could do better and claim them" ([@ 15:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=903s)).
- **If your offer sounds too good to be true, admitting flaws matters even more.** In a 2026 consult he said that making the offer "less good" makes it "more believable". On sales calls he'd open with "Listen, before I tell you about the good, let me tell you about the bad," and then list everything that sucks ([Feb 2026 consult @ 19:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1149s), [@ 19:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1182s)). He turned the flaw into a trade the customer accepts: "you can have what you want, just not when you want." That lets prospects "self-qualify" ([@ 20:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1214s)).
- **A related tactic: say who the product is not for.** He calls naming who you're *not* for "even more powerful" than naming who you are for. One of his best PS formats is "a disclaimer of who this is not for" ([@ 5:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=302s), [@ 26:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=1577s)).

**A template that follows his rules:**
> "Honestly, [real flaw #1]. [Real flaw #2]. And [real flaw #3]. **But** [the one result you want them to believe]."
> PS: If [the kind of person the flaw rules out], this isn't for you.

**Where this is uncertain**
- The vault has no numbers from him on how much admissions improve conversion. His evidence is unnamed research saying people trust someone more after they admit a bias, plus the Eminem rap-battle story. Both are illustrations, not his own test data.
- He doesn't say which flaws to leave out. All his examples are minor or don't touch the core promise (parking, smell, ugly design). It's safe to read that as "admit the flaws that don't undercut your main claim, then make that claim after the but", but that's my inference, not something he says.
- Conflict of interest: these talks promote his books and Acquisition.com.

**Short answer:** Third grade. Hormozi's rule doesn't change for an educated audience. He assumes every reader is rushed, distracted and doesn't care, so anything that makes them stop to work out what you mean loses them.

**What he's said** (all from "14 Years of Marketing Advice in 35 Minutes", 2025: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM)
- **Copy fails because readers have to stop.** "most copy doesn't convert because people have to pause to understand it and the moment they pause they stop" (@ 30:15, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=1815s)
- **He writes for the worst-case reader.** "we have to assume that the prospect is in a rush doesn't care about what you have has below a third grade reading level and is distracted" (@ 30:15)
- **A higher grade level shuts people out.** "if we want to automatically disqualify twothirds of the people who read the copy keep it at nth grade" (@ 32:07, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=1927s). His alternative is to write at third grade "if you want everyone who can read to read."
- **"you're not writing a college paper"** (@ 31:26). Good copy is copy where "the words fade into the background."
- **"fancy equals friction simple equals sales"** (@ 32:07)
- **How to do it:** "sentences small words big promises" and "few adverbs and better verbs." When short and simple pull in different directions, simple wins: "I will never prioritize concision over simplicity" (@ 32:43)

**What he does:** He runs every ad he writes through a free reading-level tool and keeps editing until it scores at third grade (@ 32:07).

**Where this is uncertain:** The vault has no source where he talks about educated or B2B readers specifically. So "it applies to business owners too" is my reading, not his words. Two things back it up:
- He doesn't limit the rule by audience. He says to assume *every* prospect is in a rush and distracted.
- The video is an ad for business owners. It runs a pitch for his free scaling roadmap ("if you're a business owner…", @ 30:50) in the middle of this exact section. That's his own buyers, getting the same plain style.

His logic for your case: an educated owner can read at a high grade level, but scrolling through an ad they won't bother to. Simple words are what let them understand you in the second they give you.

**One caveat from me:** Simple wording doesn't mean dumbed-down content. Specific numbers, real proof and industry terms your buyers use every day can stay in. Cut the long sentences and fancy words around them.

**Short answer:** No. Hormozi describes almost exactly your situation, and his answer is not to start a second or third approach. He says that kicking off parallel fixes after about 30 days, because the first one "isn't solved yet," pulls resources away from the one approach that will work but takes time. Stay with the recruiting push, and work on making it run better instead of adding new ones.

**What he's said**
- He describes your exact pattern and calls it a mistake: "I will kick off a real meaty solution to a big thing… it's 30 days later and I'll be like, oh my god, it's not solved yet. And then I'll want to try and solve it another way." His conclusion is: "me trying to solve it in two or three ways ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work but will take time" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s)).
- On putting up with the delay: "Sometimes you have to sit with the pain of an unbuilt bridge without building a second bridge" ([@ 4:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=298s)). He also says "sometimes you have to let the little fires burn" (@ 6:04).
- He'd rather make one large bet than spread out. He prefers "the sure bets on the thing that has the absolute highest leverage impact… rather than many small bets that might or might not work," and calls the alternative "death by a thousand paper cuts" (@ 6:36). He also says "you have one real bet that you can make on it. And so it's like you want to make that bet worth it" (@ 10:27).
- He thinks adding more initiatives costs the team more than leaders expect: "I promise your team's 10 times more overwhelmed" (@ 13:14).
- On compounding: "the effort that it takes to compound is the length of time you have to say no to everything else" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 22:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1378s)).
- On how to recruit: when you're short of people, he says to treat the people you want to hire as your customers. "I want you to think about sales people as your new customers or your new avatar… some of the marketing that you're going to do is to go get these guys" ([yt-o64cI6tebnU @ 21:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1305s)).

**How to use this:** He separates new bets from day-to-day tuning, like improving close rates or lead flow, which he doesn't count as extra bets. So tuning the recruiting push you already have fits his advice: run better job ads, sharpen the offer to technicians, and follow up with applicants faster. Starting two or three separate programs does not.

**What he's done:** He admits he has this habit himself. He says he gets impatient after about 30 days and starts a second approach, and that he talks about focus partly to "hammer it into my own brain." The advice comes from his own mistakes, not from a clean record of following it.

**Where this is uncertain**
- The "one thing" talk is about high-level strategy bets in general, not hiring specifically. His recruiting advice in the vault is about salespeople at a roofing company, not technicians.
- He assumes the one approach "will work but will take time." The vault has nothing from him on how to tell when a bet is actually failing rather than just slow, so it can't say how long to wait. If a month in you're getting no applicants at all, as opposed to applicants who haven't converted yet, his advice would point to fixing the recruiting offer itself. That reading is my extrapolation, not something he said.
- Much of this framing comes from books he'd just read (Ken Segall's *Insanely Simple*, Frank Slootman's book) and from Steve Jobs.

My own view: one month is short for hiring technicians. Before you change anything, it's worth checking where the push is stalling: not enough applicants, applicants who don't make it through, or offers that get turned down.

**Short answer:** About 20% monthly churn (80% retention) is average for a paid online community. Under 10% is top tier. If you keep less than 70% of members each month (30%+ churn), fix retention before anything else. Don't judge it by the overall average, though. Look at how many people make it past day 90 and month 6, because churn drops sharply at those points.

**What Hormozi has said**

All of this comes from one 2026 talk, "How to Get Your Customers to Stay FOREVER" (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q). The numbers are Skool platform averages he got from Sam, Skool's founder.

- **Benchmarks:** "the platform average across School is 80% monthly retention… the best groups have less than 10% churn, aka 90% retention month over month. The not good groups have less than 70% retention" ([@ 1:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s)).
- **When to worry:** "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever." (@ 1:39)
- **Why small improvements matter:** going from 20% to 10% churn means "you didn't just get a 10 or 12% boost, you got a double in the LTV per customer" ([@ 2:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=133s)).
- **The "biggest rule": churn falls with tenure.** Months 1–3 run at "20% plus". After 90 days "it drops to around 10% or less". By month 6 "it goes from like 10% to 2%" ([@ 3:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=233s)). So the question to ask isn't "how do I make this number go down?" It's "How do I get someone to stay past day 90? How do I get these people to stay past month six?" ([@ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=264s)).
- **A new community will look worse than it is.** If it's under 90 days old, "your churn is always going to be inflated", and somewhat less so under six months. So "don't overhaul your entire business because your month one churn sucks." Instead, "have a very specific strategy for getting people past the first month" (@ 4:24–4:57).
- **What gets people past each point:** "Day 90 is probably going to have to deliver some sort of outcome… Month six, it's usually them connecting with other people within that community." ([@ 5:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=331s))
- **What to track:** joins against cancels every month. Label the business "growing, flat, or declining" based on those two numbers ([@ 0:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=33s)).

**What he says to do if churn is high**
- **Ask why people leave:** message everyone who cancels and tag their reason. After every 20 or so cancels, fix the top one or two reasons. Also ask your longest-staying members why they stay, and do more of that.
- **Cut overwhelm:** "The number one reason people churn, outside of price, is overwhelm" (@ 9:18). Offer less, and give new members a quick win "ideally within the first 24 hours".
- **Show up every day:** owners who showed up daily "had significantly higher retention". Run one big live call a week. Introduce new members to about 10 regulars and help each one make "one real friend".
- **Add a discounted annual plan:** "annual always has lower churn than monthly… you only need to decide one time rather than 12" (@ 15:52).

**Where this is uncertain**
- These are Skool averages, and he promotes Skool and is involved with it. He says they apply to online and consumer services, not things like insurance or alarm systems.
- These are monthly figures for a monthly product, and they come from a single talk. The vault has no other source on churn to check them against.

You will always be first in line.", @ 16:25), and around outcomes, not just access to you: "They don't really want your time. They want to buy an outcome." (@ 14:12)
- **Limit it so it doesn't take over.** "just cap it… be willing to take 5 10% of your time, charge 10 times more and make enough income from that that you can take all the other money and go aggressive" (@ [15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=919s)). This is his answer to the worry about distraction.
- **The distraction risk he does warn about is overwhelming your current members.** In his own Skool community, "the number one reason that people were cancelling was overwhelm" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 11:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=662s)). His fix was to cut calls from three a week to one. So keep the $100 tier simple. Put the premium extras in the premium tier, not on top of the base offer.
- **He also tells you to focus on one bet.** He asks "what one thing if it were true 12 months from now would change everything" (@ 3:52) and warns against "building a second bridge" (@ 4:58). If your one bet this year is growing the core community, the premium tier should be a small, capped add-on and not a second business.

**What he's done:** He ran a group-training gym and took one personal-training client five days a week. That client's cash covered his own pay, so all the gym's money could go back into growth ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 1:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=97s)). At a PR company in his portfolio, he noticed that the 15% of clients who bought the top package also stayed. He rebuilt the business around them and raised prices 10x.

**Where this is uncertain:**
- The "near-100% margin" assumes the premium tier is mostly your own time. If it needs staff or vendors, the numbers get worse.
- He says he struggles with focus himself. He calls starting a second approach after about 30 days a mistake he's trying to stop.
- **Conflict of interest:** he co-founded Skool, a community platform, and his community and retention advice draws on Skool data.
- The vault has nothing specific to freelancer audiences, and no data on how many community members actually upgrade to a premium tier.
- Separately, his advice on adding a *lower* tier when your ideal customers say the price is too high ([yt--j8_YCWZ05Q @ 8:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=526s)) goes in the opposite direction, so don't mix the two up.

One caveat of my own: freelancers are often short on cash, so test whether you have premium buyers before you build much. Offering a few one-on-one slots is the cheap way to do that, and it's also what he recommends.

**Short answer:** No, not yet. Hormozi was asked almost exactly this question, and his answer was to stop treating new channels as the fix. He thinks the wall usually means your ad creative has run out, not that Meta has. He'd have you make better creative, raise conversion and add sales capacity on Meta first. He called a new channel "a little too hard for right now."

**Your situation has already been through his consult.** In Feb 2026 he advised Joel McDonald, whose travel-points coaching business was almost the same as yours. It made about $6.4M over the trailing 12 months (roughly $530k a month), and 85% of customers came from Meta. It was "hitting a ceiling at 100 grand a month," and the owner wanted to grow guest podcasting and affiliates ([yt-MH-IMJxbUY4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=100s)). Joel had spent $150k the month before and got only 10% more book sales.

**What he said**

- **Treat it as a demand problem and use his decision tree.** You can open a new channel, lower your cost per customer (better creative, a better-converting funnel, or a better offer), or just spend more. He picks the existing channel: "I feel like there's a lot more that you can work on the existing one by like a lot" ([@ 5:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=327s)). His verdict: "New channel, little too hard for right now in my opinion" ([@ 24:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1446s)).
- **Creative is what caps spend.** "the creative unlock is usually why someone gets limited" ([@ 12:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=720s)). Meta shows your ads to the most interested people first. Past that group, "as soon as you hit you try to break through this wall, your CPA goes up because the new creative's not good enough" ([@ 13:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=786s)). For a broad offer he thought spend could go to "100,000 plus a day" ([@ 5:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=327s)).
- **How he'd get more creative:**
  - **Customer videos.** Reward customers for posting their own videos and test 20–30 of them a week: "every week we just blast off 30 videos up there and we see where the winners are" ([@ 8:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=523s)).
  - **Organic first.** Post short videos without paying, then "add a 5-second CTA at the end, and then run that as an ad" ([@ 13:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=820s)).
  - **Variations of winners.** He calls this "kaleidoscoping": many versions of a winning ad's visuals with the copy kept the same. "once we have the winners, we kaleidoscope the hell out of them" ([@ 10:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=623s)). He says one of his companies spends a couple hundred thousand dollars a day using only three hooks over five years.
  - **Different people in the ads.** People buy from people who look like them, so a wider range of faces may reach new groups of buyers. He labels this a guess with no data behind it ([@ 14:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=885s)).
- **Sell harder to the leads you already get.** Score leads, call the best ones first, hire more salespeople and give them a parallel dialer: "I think you need to increase your number of sales people" ([@ 21:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1279s)).
- **Spend more only when you can trust the numbers.** If the return holds, spend "as many dollars as you possibly could." If you can't tell, "you have a data problem. So, you got to go make sure the attribution's right" ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 11:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=681s)).
- **If you do add affiliates later, build an offer for the partners.** "Referrals everyone promises, no one delivers" ([@ 25:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1550s)). His model has partners sell a cheap, high-margin product of yours and keep the money, and you then sell them your main offer. He warns it is "a less scalable option" ([@ 28:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1682s)). Pick one partner channel, not several ("I don't think you're going to be able to do both of these"), with one person on it full-time ([@ 29:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=1779s)). He ranked it below fixing the funnel and the ads.
- **Running several fixes at once is a known mistake.** "me trying to solve it in two or three ways ends up just pulling resources from the one way that I know will work but will take time" ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 6:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=364s)).

**Where this is uncertain**
- His advice comes from one consult, and Joel's product is very visual (travel). Hormozi says less visual businesses are harder to make creative for and need an emotional angle instead.
- The idea that one good enough ad could convert everyone is, in his words, his "theoretical view of the world," not data.
- Joel's economics were tight: a book sold at a loss, about 6 months to break even, and a 1.4:1 ratio of customer value to acquisition cost. If your margins look different, how hard to push Meta may also differ.
- The vault has nothing from him about podcasts as a growth channel. He also profits from this advice: these consult videos pitch Acquisition.com.

**My own view:** his answer assumes your offer is broad. If it's narrow, check whether the wall is real audience saturation before betting everything on creative. A cheap test is to measure how much ad fatigue and frequency rose during the $150k-type months.

**Short answer:** No. Hormozi would say you're about to make it worse. Your two cancel reasons are the top two churn drivers he names, price and overwhelm. Extra trainings and calls do nothing for price and add to the overwhelm. He'd cut the offer down instead, and handle price with an annual plan, plus a cheaper tier if your ideal members are the ones saying it costs too much.

**What he's said**

- **At 30% churn, retention is your main problem.** "if less than seven out of 10 people want to stay on a monthly basis, you probably need to work on your retention more than anything else. It'll be the highest ROI lever." ([source @ 1:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=99s)) Halving churn doubles lifetime value.

- **"Can't keep up" means overwhelm, and adding things makes it worse.** "The number one reason people churn, outside of price, is overwhelm. It is the churn driver. And this is why doing less can often retain more." ([@ 9:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=558s)) His reasoning: "When you have five things that you pay for, but you only use one, you feel like you're only getting 20% of the value. If for the same price, you just offer that one thing, people feel like they're getting 100% of the value." ([@ 10:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=622s)) About added features that went unused: "all we did is we gave them more reason to cancel because they never used it" ([@ 10:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=654s)).

- **This also answers "too expensive."** If members use one of five things, they feel they get 20% of the value, so $99 feels like too much. More bonuses lower that share further.

- **Price complaints: check who is making them.** "if your ideal customer say the price is the issue, then you can add a lower tier or a standard plan. If non-ideal people say it's too expensive, just ignore it. That means that the price is actually acting as a good filter" ([@ 8:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=526s)). Skool added a $9 tier under its $99 one for hobbyists.

- **Add an annual plan now.** "annual always has lower churn than monthly and it's because you only need to decide one time rather than 12" ([@ 15:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=952s)). He suggests about 16–17% off, which works out to "buy 10 get two".

- **Work on the first 90 days, not the average.** Churn is highest in months 1–3. It drops to about 10% after day 90 and about 2% by month six ([@ 3:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=233s)). His suggestions: put a fast win where new members hit it "ideally within the first 24 hours" ([@ 13:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=786s)), and give busy members a "start here / weekly cadence flow" with the extra depth kept optional.

- **Find the one thing people stay for, then cut.** Ask members: "if I were to delete everything, what one thing would you fight for?" ([@ 11:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=686s)) Ask your longest-staying members why they stay, and do more of that: "If you can only do one thing that gets people to stay, why would you do five?" ([@ 7:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=428s))

- **Live calls: one a week.** He does think live calls help retention. His default is "one big thing per week" plus a best-of post ([@ 15:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=919s)), not several.

**What he's done:** His own Skool Games community had overwhelm as its top cancel reason. He cut the calls "from three a week to one", moved the big download from monthly to quarterly, and turned off some app features ([2025 talk @ 11:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=695s)). That is the opposite of your plan. He also mentions a community that cut churn from 30% to 5% by deleting content, though that is someone else's business he's describing.

**Where this is uncertain**

- Whether to add a cheaper tier or ignore the price complaints depends on whether the people saying it are your ideal members. You'll have to check your own cancel data for that.
- His benchmarks come from Skool platform data, and he is involved with Skool, so he isn't neutral on it.
- The vault has no case that matches your numbers exactly. Everything above comes from his general retention advice applied to your situation.
